items.text: Milestone: "the first year in which we have spent more physically on prevention than we have on treatment", and the gap between supplements and OTC will widen [00:20] (photo 2).

Money is moving to premium dietary supplements, through line extensions, brand actions and M&A; he sees "about eight to $9 billion in motion", some from venture capital and private equity outside health [00:20].

Healthspan as a funnel: the edge (SKU names directly on age and life stage, including mitochondrial) is niche, growing and earns a premium; broader healthspan wording appears on cheap and expensive products alike; protection messages (immune, antioxidant) cover about half the shelf [00:20].

Ingredient life cycle: proof of benefit, then premium, then popularity, then price war. Magnesium forms "turned into footballs" on price, while L-threonate, the cognitive form, still holds a premium; "popularity is the death knell on premium" [00:20] (photo 3).

NAD+ is losing its premium as it goes mainstream (US price index 1.84 in 2024, 1.43 in 2026 to date); postbiotics lead what queues behind it, with share up 48% and a price index of 2.83 [00:20] (photo 4).
IM8 is the fastest year-one growth he has seen: one product of 90 ingredients positioned to replace 16 supplements, with year-two revenue guidance of USD 220 to 230 million [00:20] (photo 7).

Concern about ageing starts younger: retired respondents mostly began thinking seriously about it in their 60s (36% on the Retired bar), people in full-time work mostly in their 30s; she called it "a generational shift" [00:04] (photo 1).

The younger the respondent, the less they credit genetics and the more they credit supplements: genetics from 39% at 65 plus down to 21% in the youngest group; supplements from 20% at 25 to 34 down to 12% at 65 plus [00:04].
"[1 in] 4 is actively pursuing [anti]-ageing": 16% want to prevent premature ageing and 11% to reverse it, beside 52% who want to age slowly and healthily [00:04] (photo 2).

Energy, stamina and strength is in the top three concerns of every age band shown, for men and women; mobility, joint and bone health is in the top three of every band from 35 to 44 up for both, and from 25 to 34 for women (photo 3).
Trust is the gap: the first answer to "What's your biggest hesitation about taking longevity supplements?" was not enough proof; 36% already take supplements to counteract natural ageing [00:04].

Brands are moving from selling supplements to managing biological ageing: Life Extension sells ageing blood tests to take before and after supplements, and she gave Novos as "Another similar example" of a move "from supplement brand to health intelligence company" [00:04] (photo 4).
Starbucks' 15 g protein cold foam is his example of the bigger market: Starbucks say one in seven coffees now provides 15 g of protein. A bigger market is not more of the same market [00:00].

Brands are not just mitigating whey prices but going through a "structural reset". New products that cut whey reliance and a shift into creatine, energy and fibre are the "top priority for brands" [00:00] (photo 6).

More "whey hybrids" (sold as whey, blended with milk, soy or yeast to cut cost) launched in the last 12 months than ever; whey milkshakes and whey plus collagen are the next pillars [00:00] (photo 9).
Plant protein still underdelivers on taste. It should sell itself as a very good protein, not as plant [00:00] (photo 10).
Gummies are the fastest-growing creatine format by new launches: 8.0% of creatine products, 36.2% of them added in the last six months, with "lots of conjecture about stability" [00:00] (photo 14).
A quarter of creatine products use a branded ingredient, most of it from one supplier, and he said there is a race to follow; pre-workout is highest at 53% [18:50] (photo 27).
The core constraint: cheese production grows about 1.5% a year, while whey protein demand grows over 10%. He called it the most important conclusion of the talk [00:16] (photo 7).
Producers chose isolate. Over five years WPI grew 15.0% a year and WPC80 1.5%; clear WPI is now about a quarter of all isolate (photo 9).
Between 25 August and 4 November 2026, WPC80 fell 40.7% to €16.00/kg and WPI 20.3% to €25.50/kg, while MPC85 rose 13.5% to €15.80/kg (photo 18).
New capacity will not close the gap: he forecast WPI at 7 to 11% a year and WPC80 at 4 to 7% to 2030, and both cannot reach the top of their range [00:16] (photo 11).
Mainstream buyers choose on taste and texture, not protein source, and whey is the easiest protein to make taste good [00:16].
For buyers: "Don't try to time the market. Keep inventory steady. Whey will be expensive." (photo 20)
More than 1,000 misleading food posts by influencers were counted in a recent report, with supplements the most frequent subject [00:01].

Tonic runs itself as "a media business that happens to sell vitamins": 99% of its content is not about its products, and it has 1.9 million followers and about 70 million views a month [01:00], [03:24].
AG1 found that talking about trials and third-party testing did not land: "people didn't care". Too much evidence fails at the top of the funnel; the science sits mid-funnel [04:17], [18:30].

Clearcast rejected "the best version of you", "a better version of you" and "a slightly better version of you" before approving "Ever wondered what life would be like with a little extra help?" Julian's lesson: "creative constraint is a very powerful way to deliver better communication" [18:30].
Brands bear most responsibility for their influencers' health claims in most jurisdictions; the answer is training, contracts and briefing [28:27].
Athletes are "probably the most impressionable group": they believe a claim of "up to 10% better performance" applies to them personally [32:33].

Women started with less muscle glycogen than men but finished similarly depleted. The gap was under 5 g in the gastrocnemius, comes from dosing per kilogram, and has no practical bearing on guidelines [00:00].
At 120 g of carbohydrate an hour, the crossover from carbohydrate to fat was completely prevented over two hours, in both sexes; at 60 g it came after about an hour [00:00] (photo 4) (photo 6).

Men and women oxidise carbohydrate taken during exercise at comparable rates, rising with dose (120 > 90 > 60 g); at 120 g some individuals oxidised 80 to 100 percent of what they took [00:00] (photo 7).
Running economy improved by two to 3% at 120 g an hour, against the 4% Nike claimed for the Vaporfly; he is "pretty sure" this is part of why running records are falling [00:00] (photo 9).
Women reported more gastrointestinal symptoms, "which may be due to anatomical differences in colon length"; individual variation warrants personalised fuelling [00:00] (photo 9).
The biggest barrier is educational, in a world where under-fuelling has been prevalent; he does not believe in fuelling to the menstrual cycle [00:00] (photo 20).
Brands have three responses to whey costs: raise the price, shrinkflation, or smarter formulation with protein blends, which she called the most elegant and a way to stand out on shelf [00:10].
Launches combining whey and collagen are growing at almost 17.5 percent a year; a 10 g collagen plus 10 g whey product was her example [00:10].
Collagen supply is spread across bovine, porcine, chicken and fish, and its historical prices fluctuate far less than whey's [00:10].
Whey and collagen are "no competitors": whey for muscle, Peptan (rich in hydroxyproline, glycine and proline) for ligaments, tendons, joints and bone [00:10].
In 22 men over three weeks of training, 25 g whey plus 20 g Peptan gave the same recovery and performance as 45 g whey [00:10].
20 g Peptan with vitamin C for seven days gave 28% less muscle soreness and 13% faster muscle recovery than placebo after 150 jumps [00:10].

Three segments of everyday athlete: "inspired by" (habits, feeling better, food first), "driven by" (measured progress, nutrient timing around training) and "live by" (optimisers who plan the whole 24 hours around training) [00:54].
Most of their 8,000 daily training-app users train at 6:00 in the morning, so Marchon put carbohydrate into a pre-workout for people who will not eat toast or porridge first [00:54], [04:00].
Awareness is high but understanding lags: gym-goers talk confidently about products they saw in an ad without knowing why, so "education is really critical at this stage" [05:29].
Liam: creatine is "here to stay" and the research is moving into cognition; for ingredient suppliers the challenge is format, meaning stability in water, gummies and other formats [08:24].
When Marchon surveyed its gym members, the number one struggle was still hitting their daily protein requirement [16:50].
Five years out, Liam's bet is "formats that improve compliance": gummies, jellies, powders, RTDs, and convenience [22:11].
In the UK, 6.1% currently take GLP-1s, 5.7% have taken them and 15.1% are considering them: together about 18.4 million people [00:08].
Current users are not the obesity population the drugs were designed for: 56% female, 63% Gen X or Millennial, 63% ABC1, and 74% happy to pay more for quality [00:08].
Two thirds expect to spend the same or more on food and drink, and near 60% are likely to increase their supplement use; creatine was "maybe slightly higher" than expected [00:08].
The openings are side effects, nutrition gaps (muscle loss, difficulty eating enough protein and nutrients) and lapsed users, with a malnutrition risk for people who eat less without care [00:08].
He cited a British Medical Association study: people are four times more likely to regain weight lost with GLP-1 than weight lost by traditional methods [00:08].
Putting GLP-1 on pack is "a kind of a health claim", so retailer support such as Boots' GLP-1 bays matters [00:08].
GLP-1 drugs give weight loss of "between five to 15%", but users lose body weight rather than only body fat, and muscle loss "can lead to sarcopenia" [00:15].
The GLP-1 supplement boom brought "some high-profile lawsuits", regulatory clampdowns and lower consumer confidence [00:15].
Proteins have an "undisputed effect" on GLP-1 secretion, depending on quality and amino acid profile [00:15].
Berberine, cinnamon and bitter compounds have mechanisms but "mild to modest" effects and few human studies [00:15].
In his centre's appetite trial, potato protein and whey protein isolate raised GLP-1 significantly and equally [00:15].
A mulberry extract significantly raised GLP-1 at 180 minutes and significantly reduced appetite and food noise; the paper is due to be submitted next week [00:15].
Brett: GLP-1 trends are "accelerations of existing macro trends", and retailers now want sports nutrition across the supermarket, not only on the health fixture [28:46].

Few products put GLP-1 overtly on pack: Myprotein builds need-state bundles rather than a labelled GLP-1 range, and Boots' "GLP-1 friendly" bays let it be present without the wording [29:57], [30:32], [51:57].
Brett: clear protein is "performing extremely well" in retail, and clear protein plus collagen is "just a sweet spot for this this consumer", with retail launches coming [35:09], [43:51].
Nick: plant protein's barrier is taste; it has got better but is "never quite as good as we truly expect for the majority of people" [37:08].
Nick: creatine has become "almost like a tier one ingredient", adopted by women, ageing consumers and weight-management users [38:42].
Ed: people who simply eat less risk missing key nutrients, with a risk of RED-S and deficiencies; for low appetite he puts protein first, then carbohydrate, then micronutrients [32:49], [34:13].
Consumers buy "energy and vitality" and "cellular health"; the hallmarks of ageing are "for this people in this room" [00:00].
Of about 300 products coded, 9% refer to the hallmarks and only 4%, he thinks, put them in lead copy [00:00].
"You don't sell one product in 2026": brands sell a routine of about three products, and an ingredient is sold on how it fits the customer's product system [00:00].
Longevity products are among the most expensive per serve; the creatine median is about 50 cents a serve, and the same ingredient labelled longevity can be "a hell of a lot more expensive" [00:00].
Longevity is shifting into sports nutrition (Centenarian, linked to Sergio Ramos), and cellular claims are entering hydration [00:00].
PeptiStrong is a fava bean protein hydrolysate; the speaker says its peptides target mTOR (muscle building) and NF kappa B (inflammation) [03:56].

Immobilisation trial (Netherlands, males only): the control was milk protein concentrate, not a placebo; muscle lost and regained was the same, but strength came all the way back to baseline and FSR was higher with PeptiStrong [03:56].
KGK trial (Canada, untrained men and women): stronger quicker at day 28, kept at day 56; GDF15 fell with training load; bone mineral content rose, "a kind of a serendipitous finding" [03:56].
Nuritas positions PeptiStrong as a booster of protein and a partner for creatine, leucine and HMB: "we're not competing with protein" [03:56].
On-pack claims rest on EFSA protein claims; the regulatory manager has been "creatively defining" others [13:50].
Commercial map: Vivatis formulates for Central and Eastern Europe, Nuritas has been active in Poland for six months, and it is developing a product with Tantus [13:50].
Ubiquinol is the active form of CoQ10; the speaker says the converting enzyme diaphorase is no longer available as you get older, from about 30 [00:00].
300 mg of Q10 gives the same blood ubiquinol as 90 mg of ubiquinol; at 300, 600 or 900 mg of Q10 the body cannot convert more than 300 mg [00:00].
Kaneka's dose: 100 mg a day for a normal person; up to 300 mg for statin users, energy, fertility and stress [00:00].
Formats: pure ubiquinol for softgels, gel pills and gummies; a microencapsulated form for other dosage formats [00:00].
Kaneka is pushing ubiquinol into active nutrition: "energy and sports" among its study areas, and a partnership with Borussia Dortmund's women's football team [00:00].
NovaSol is a micellar technology: lipophilic core, hydrophilic surface, water-soluble, protected from stomach acid, with no chemical change to the active [00:18].
Each NovaSol formulation is unique to its ingredient; it is a liquid concentrate for capsules, shots and combined capsules [00:18].
GVR, a US direct-to-consumer longevity brand, built Mind, Q Power and Glow on the same micellar resveratrol with different NovaSol actives, in vegetarian softgels [00:18].
MSM is 34% sulfur by weight, a source of sulfur and methyl groups; supplementation "has shown" effects on joint and skin health and exercise recovery, the speaker said [10:40].
Balchem has 33 active research projects; methylfolate is a new ingredient it hopes to bring to Europe soon [09:04].
The gap he names is anabolic resistance: ageing muscle uses protein less well, hence the move from 0.8 to 1.2 g of protein, and "hardly any ingredient" addresses it [00:00].
Wild Rhodiola rosea is overharvested, adulterated with other species and, he said, listed as endangered in 2023: a supply risk for any brand built on it [00:00].
Trial: double-blind, placebo-controlled, 140 untrained adults aged 55 to 75; both arms trained and were given protein; 400 mg of Rhosera once a day in the morning [00:00].
Delayed-onset muscle soreness fell 46% in men and 52% in women, against 18% and 11% on placebo; the human publication is "in progress" [00:00].
No EFSA claim on rhodiola; brands "borrow" magnesium or vitamin B claims on fatigue [00:00].
The standard brief is "impossible"; judge a launch on whether they will remember it, whether you can make it and whether you can prove it [00:01].

items.text: A trend does not change anything on its own; the product has to reach the market and become part of a daily routine [00:31].
The question is not what else to add to a formula but what makes sense and why [01:05].
Simplicity first: format, dosage and ease of use matter because consistent use is the point [02:09].
Tantus wants long-term supplier relationships rather than transactional orders, for access to research, technical information, formulation expertise and new ideas [03:09].

Concept one: creatine reframed for longevity, a chewable tablet with Solabia, three grams of creatine with "400 grams" of a hesperidin-based ingredient (Otter's summary gives 400 mg), tried at Solabia's stand [04:45].
Fermotein is one ingredient with 50% complete protein, 30% prebiotic fibre (chitin and chitosan) and spermidine at about 1700 mg per kilo, used mainly in active nutrition [00:00].
First mycelium protein with EFSA approval, "since the summer of this year" after five years; also approved in Singapore, with Australia and Canada pending [00:00].
Market entry was the US "all-in-one nutrition" segment, between protein powder and meal replacement; Ka'Chava is the model, "super profitable", in Walmart and online [00:00].
In Europe the nearest category is still meal replacement, not all-in-one nutrition; he expects it to come and asked the CDMOs present to embrace it [00:00].

Evidence: prebiotic studies, a positive effect on GLP-1, and a C. elegans study in which Fermotein increased nematode lifespan by 22%; a human biological ageing clock trial with Wageningen University is planned for quarter one [00:00].

Customers do not buy the mechanism; they buy how they feel and keep feeling. The retailer's recurring questions are when will I feel it, what will I feel, can I measure it, and how much does it cost [00:25].
H&B's biggest own-label sellers have a clearly communicated benefit (joint function, joint comfort, brain function); products that recite clinical literature do not sell as well [00:25].
NAD: over 1000 customers surveyed and "not a single one knew what NAD was"; outcome-level data for NR and NMN is "very very limited" [00:25].
Cheap, evidence-rich interventions (fibre, vitamin D, calcium, protein) beat novel technologies on evidence and cost; vitamin D costs about two cents per 10 microgram serving [00:25].
US shelves in the last six months are "protein plus fiber"; he gave about 9% lower coronary heart disease risk for every seven grams of fibre [00:25].
When a benefit shows in trials at four, six or eight weeks, H&B can sometimes put that timescale on pack [00:25].

The market is framed as three sides, brands, manufacturers and ingredient suppliers, with Grand View Research's forecast of over 12 percent growth a year to more than 60 billion dollars by 2030 [00:13].
The cost of today's process is operational (hours organising inquiries, hunting agreements in email threads) and lost opportunity (offers never received, inquiries never answered) [01:50].
One inquiry reaches all manufacturers (or suppliers) in the category; offers come back in one structure, "two offers or 15", ready to compare [02:46].
For suppliers and manufacturers: inquiries are matched to what you can produce, so you see opportunities that today never find you [02:46].
Every company is verified before joining; the security module answers losing control of information once it sits in an inbox [07:42].
Pawel Gruszczynski (Remedy, the conference organiser) is strategic advisor and board member of the project [02:46].

Matt: trials in this industry study healthy people for short periods, so effects look small; he would run high-dose studies in people with real problems and publish, because consumers will find it through chatbots [02:52].
Alex: consumers want evidence but not the EFSA wording; "throwing the kitchen sink" (90 plus ingredients, 35 claims) muddles the message; do a few things well for a defined audience [08:33].

Joanna: EU food law and the claims regulation were written for vitamin C and D; innovators must combine what is legally possible with showing what trials found; food law should be "a shield", not "a heartbreak" [05:36].
Matt: same safety package, three years longer approval in Europe than the US; cost today, income later, so the delay "almost makes the innovation impossible" [14:53].
Matt: fish oil supply is collapsing for aquaculture now and reaches supplement shelves next summer; aquaculture buys the alternatives with higher willingness to pay [18:48].
Alex: H&B holds up to nine months of pre-purchased stock on core lines; shoppers give three or four seconds at shelf, so protect the claim they buy (heart, eye) and find the alternative [19:36].
Consumers say they do not feel informed about probiotics; the category has too many options and not enough clarity [00:24].
ingredients: Akkermansia (heard as "Acromancia"; a US brand built on it)

items.text: Rule 1: 50, 80 or 100 billion CFU on shelf means nothing to the consumer; numbers alone no longer build trust, so be the proven expert in a niche, as a US Akkermansia brand does for metabolic health and weight management [03:59].
ingredients: Akkermansia (heard as "Acromancia"; a US brand built on it)

items.text: Rule 2: talk about feeding what the consumer already has, fibres and plant diversity, which they can see and act on; fibre brands lead this language [03:59].

items.text: Rule 3: early adopters measure with microbiome tests and apps; mass-market consumers keep buying only when they feel a difference, so brands now set expectations for one week and one month [03:59].

items.text: Rule 4: consumers stick with formats they like; Poppi is her example of a product designed around the consumer rather than the ingredient [03:59].

items.text: Novonesis pitches to CMOs and CDMOs directly: probiotic solutions "already supported by research, market experience, and technical know-how", with the aim of a product the consumer will trust and repurchase, not only an ingredient sale [00:42].
Science is strain specific; some strains have limited documentation, others decades of study, and documented strains protect the reputation of the brand the manufacturer makes [00:42].

Four probiotic trends: more specialised needs, professional-recommended probiotics, applications beyond gut health, digital channels and emerging markets; "probiotic are no longer a niche category" [00:42].

Lactoflorene: partnership since the early 2000s, started by an Italian requirement of at least 1 billion CFU in a limited-volume cap; Novonesis gave the potency and stability; core formula unchanged for almost 20 years; a clinical study on the finished product beyond what Italy demanded [09:06].

Lactoflorene is third in Italy with around a 7% share; the three reasons given were clinical evidence, delivery innovation (the MCAP system for liquid shots) and formats for different ages and occasions [09:06].
The partnership's value beyond ingredients: formulation expertise, consumer and marketing support, access to a pipeline of new bio-solutions [13:10].

Its pitch as a CDMO is speed and flexibility: a low time to market, working in synergy with the customer, and setting up a new kind of production if asked ("If you have got something crazy, we like to do that") [00:00].

Offer: probiotics, postbiotics and customised mixtures; "culture science" strains with clinical studies and "culture select" strains screened to EFSA requirements, more than 30 species; strain development for third parties [00:00].

CA15 (women's health): patented strain, 2022; six-woman exploratory study then 200 women; "10 mil per capsule" for 10 days, one-month washout; he reported reduced symptoms and, one month after intake stopped, 98% restored pH and 92% negative amine test [00:00].
Symbio (healthy ageing): 1:1 paracasei and rhamnosus from Marche centenarians; a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in 97 subjects, "five mil" daily, six months [00:00].

Symbio results as he gave them: more lactobacilli, bifidobacteria and butyrate, a 43% reduction in hs-CRP ("a marker of inflammaging"), reduced TNF, improved IGF-1 "correlated with the protein synthesis as well as the maintenance of the muscle mass", and "a decrease in the reduction in the length" of telomeres [00:00].
Sacco has recently invested in clinical studies and patents in two areas, women's health and healthy ageing [00:00].

Chewable probiotic tablets: a polyol-based platform with low water content and water activity, compressed at low force, sweet without sugar; probiotics survive the process; shown in a real Favea product [00:01].
